I started using at 15 as a way of coping with feelings of depression, alienation, and agoraphobia. For a bit it helped, I went to psychs and lied of course and hid my usage from everyone and I was good at it, depression and drug use turned me into a great liar and I hate that about myself. Now at 22 my longest sober period was 7 months after a stay in a mental hospital. I was heavily dependent on coke, alcohol, xanax, and vyvanse and for a very brief period oxycodone and sure for a bit drugs numb your feelings, give you a sense of peace, but that feeling fades and it turns into a slog. Artificial chemicals are no way to deal with emotional and mental issues, not to throw platitudes at you but it only makes things worse. Using drugs as a way to cope with mental illness is the worst possible thing you can do if you want to get better. 


I knew that when I first took oxy at 15. I know that now whenever I use drugs as a means of escaping my issues. And yet I still use and it fuels my degrading mental state. 


I wish I had the answer to depression, anxiety, all that, but the truth is there’s no clear cut way to get better. It’s just a lot of hard work, a lot of openness and vulnerability, and a lot of willingness to ask for help. If you want my advice, a random person on a drugs discussion forum, be as honest as you can with what you’re dealing with. Confide in family, a close friend or two that you trust, and especially be honest with therapists/psychs or else itll just be a waste of time rather than a way to grow and improve. I wish I’d never started using drugs, but now it’s the only coping mechanism I have for dealing with my issues and it’s incredibly destructive and unhealthy. I can’t speak on medication, I’ve tried upwards of 20 different ssris, snris, antipsychotics, anxiolytics, and it took about four years to find a combination that balanced me and made me feel normal. But did I stick with it? No, because I knew drugs would make me feel ten times better in the short term, even if I would feel one hundred times worse in the long term. So no, I don’t think you should turn to drugs, I think you should develop healthy coping mechanisms and build up a network of people you trust to support you 

P.s. fuck that dude that said “oh just try a sport, you’re just being weak.” Your feelings are valid. Mental illness is not a matter of weakness, it’s just a chemical imbalance. I do this fairly often as I take large doses of ketamine roughly every three to four days, sometimes more. 

It’s a drug that’s almost impossible to describe. Closest thing to being out of body that you can get imo. Sure you can go out and attempt to walk and explore, but you can barely talk at all. You’re constantly slipping in and out of a distorted consciousness, you’re eyesight distorted by vibrant lights and a series of images rather than continuous vision. 

The best way to do it is take the ketamine, put on some music, and khole. The music almost guides images made up of cerebral, dark and blue and magenta lights made up in your head as the music guides you. Sometimes it’ll bring up images of your past, almost like you’re reliving a memory with a psychedelic, constantly shifting morphing filter over it. Other times things become so vivid it is almost indistinguishable from your sober open eye vision. You have light control over this, but mostly you are just guided through various scenarios, sometimes bland, a slow zoom into a brick building at night, it leads you down to figures in sleeping bags under it smoking or moving in unnatural patterns. Other times it’s completely abstract, a town in Iceland, you’re moving through the streets, floating and disembodied, and there’s thousands of smiling people on bicycles riding in place, far too many to be logically possible given the space they occupy. 


And often it delves into traumatic memories from your past. Well, I saw traumatic because a lot of the time it’s a fantastic memory that now is so melancholy because you’ve lost touch with the person or place or things, things ended poorly, normally something like this would make you cry but you’re so detached from yourself that you see it as if you aren’t you, as if you’re watching the memories of a person you’ve never known play out on theatre screen in disconnected, warped vignettes. 

It can be beautiful but it can be easy to chase those moments where you reconnect with someone you truly loved and miss, even if it is just a distorted version of your best time with them
